new_paragraphs: Indian cuisine scales beautifully, which is why it anchors so many big occasions. For weddings and sangeets, a lavish buffet of biryani, curries and live chaat feeds a large guest list without losing warmth. For corporate Indian catering in Dubai — office lunches, Diwali gatherings, client dinners and conference breaks — we build balanced, crowd-safe menus that travel and hold well. For private party catering and home celebrations, live dosa or tikka counters bring theatre right into the villa. Indian catering for events in Dubai works because the food is generous by nature: shareable, aromatic and portioned neatly across a hundred guests or a table of ten. add_block.new_heading: The full Indian menu, course by course
new_paragraphs: This is the working list the chefs build from, laid out in the order an Indian event is served in Dubai. Nobody takes all of it. A buffet is assembled out of these sections, a plated dinner pulls three or four courses from them, and a drop-off order narrows to the dishes that travel well. Send the occasion and the guest mix and a shortlist comes back against your date.
Welcome drinks, on arrival
An Indian menu opens with a named drink, not a soft-drink tray. Three to six is normal.
Jal Jeera: chilled cumin, mint and tamarind cooler.
Shikanji: North Indian lime with black salt and roasted cumin.
Aam Ka Panna: raw green mango with mint and jaggery.
Masala Chaach: spiced buttermilk with cumin, ginger and coriander.
Rose Sharbat: rose syrup poured over chilled water or milk.
Sweet Lassi: whisked yoghurt with sugar and cardamom.
Kesar Lassi: saffron and pistachio lassi.
Mango Lassi: ripe mango blended through yoghurt.
Paan Lassi: betel leaf and gulkand, the closing flavour served at the door.
Thandai: almond, fennel and rose milk.
Adrak Elaichi Masala Chai: ginger and cardamom chai brewed to order.
Tandoori Chai: chai finished in a fire-heated clay cup at the counter.
Cutting Chai: strong Mumbai-style half glass.
Filter Coffee: South Indian decoction coffee pulled between tumbler and dabarah.
Bombay Sunrise: mango, orange and pomegranate, no alcohol.
Shorba
One or two, poured for seated dinners and for winter events outdoors.
Tamatar Dhaniya ka Shorba: tomato and fresh coriander broth.
Murg Shorba: clear chicken broth with whole spices.
Dal Palak Soup: lentil and spinach, thick enough to stand as a course.
Palak Soup: spinach, finished with cream or with coconut milk on a vegan menu.
Lemon Coriander Broth: light clear soup, the one that suits a summer room.
Lentil Soup: plain tempered lentils for a mixed table.
Chaat and street food
Runs as a buffet section or, better, as a manned counter with the puris cracked and filled in front of the guest.
Pani Puri (vegan): puris cracked and filled with spiced water in front of the guest.
Bhel Puri: puffed rice, sev and tamarind, tossed to order so it stays crisp.
Sev Puri: flat puris topped with potato, chutneys and fine sev.
Papri Chaat: crisp papri under yoghurt, chickpeas and two chutneys.
Dahi Puri: puris filled with potato and sweetened yoghurt.
Dahi Bhalla: soft lentil dumplings soaked in chilled whisked yoghurt.
Dahi Sev Batata Puri: the Mumbai version, potato and yoghurt under a sev blanket.
Samosa Chaat: samosa crushed under chole, yoghurt and chutneys.
Aloo Tikki Chaat: griddled potato patty served with chole and chutneys.
Ragda Pattice: potato patties in a white-pea ragda.
Raj Kachori: the large stuffed kachori, cracked and filled at the counter.
Palak Patta Chaat: crisp fried spinach leaves with yoghurt and chutney.
Chana Chaat: spiced chickpeas with onion, tomato and lime.
Vada Pav with Green Chutney: the Mumbai potato vada in a soft pav.
Dabeli: sweet-spiced potato pav with pomegranate and peanuts.
Misal Pav: sprouted-bean curry under farsan, served with pav.
Pav Bhaji: mashed vegetable bhaji with butter-griddled pav.
Chole Bhature: Punjabi chickpeas with a puffed fried bhatura.
Matar Kulcha: white peas with a griddled kulcha.
Dhokla: steamed gram-flour cake tempered with mustard seed.
Khandvi: rolled gram-flour and yoghurt ribbons.
Dal Pakwan: Sindhi chana dal with crisp pakwan, a breakfast dish that works at night.
Vegetarian starters, from the tandoor
Two on a short menu, four or more on a premium one.
Paneer Tikka: char-marked paneer in five marinades — Tandoori, Achaari, Malai, Hariyali or Zaafrani.
Paneer Hilltop: paneer in a green herb and cheese marinade.
Khumb Tikka: whole mushrooms marinated and finished in the tandoor.
Tandoori Malai Broccoli: broccoli florets in a cream and cheese marinade.
Hara Bara Kebab (vegan): spinach, pea and potato patty.
Aloo Tikki: shallow-fried spiced potato patty.
Aloo Bonda: gram-flour battered potato ball.
Punjabi Samosa: the large potato and pea samosa.
Vegetable Samosa: the smaller mixed-vegetable one, cut for passing.
Green Pea Kachori (vegan): flaky kachori stuffed with spiced green peas.
Vegetable Pakora (vegan): mixed vegetable fritters fried to order.
Masala Vada: crushed chana dal fritter, South Indian.
Kothimbir Vadi: Maharashtrian coriander and gram-flour cake, steamed then fried.
Corn Palak Tikki: sweetcorn and spinach patty.
Soya Bean Tikki: soya granule and potato patty.
Vegetable Shami Kabab: soft griddled kebab bound with chana dal.
Vegetable Kathi Roll (vegan): griddled paratha rolled around spiced vegetables.
Beetroot Galouti: the Lucknowi melt-in-the-mouth kebab, made with beetroot.
Vegetable Manchurian Balls: Indo-Chinese fried vegetable balls in a dark sauce.
Chilli Cheese Toast: griddled cheese and green chilli toast.
Kebabs and non-vegetarian starters
Skewered and cooked in the tandoor, or seared on the tawa at a counter.
Chicken Malai Tikka: cream, cheese and cardamom marinade, no colouring.
Zaafrani Murg Tikka: saffron-marinated chicken tikka.
Lasuni Chicken Tikka Bites: garlic-forward, cut small for a counter.
Murg Hungama: spiced chicken tikka with a real chilli edge.
Tangdi Kebab: whole marinated drumsticks straight off the tandoor.
Chicken Tandoori: the classic on the bone, quartered for a buffet.
Bhatti Da Murgh: Punjabi clay-oven chicken, heavy on ajwain.
Mount Road Chicken 65: Chennai-style fried chicken with curry leaf.
Chicken Manchurian Bites: Indo-Chinese, tossed in a dark sauce to order.
Butter Chicken Spring Rolls: butter chicken rolled and fried, a canapé format.
Mutton Seekh Kebab: minced mutton skewered and cooked over charcoal or gas.
Sheekh Kebab: the same skewer in beef or chicken.
Chapli Kebab: flat Peshawari-style minced kebab, in beef or lamb.
Tawa Boti Lamb Kebab: lamb boti seared on the flat iron at the station.
Mini Mutton Galouti Kebab on Crispy Naan: the Lucknowi kebab served as one bite.
Bhuna Gosht Dry: slow-bhuna mutton, served dry as a starter.
Amritsari Fish Bites: ajwain-battered fried fish.
Fish Koliwada: Mumbai-style red-marinated fried fish.
Fish Tikka: fish marinated and finished in the tandoor.
Prawn Tandoori: whole prawns, skewered and grilled.
Chicken or Lamb Samosa: minced meat samosa, cut small.
Salads, raita, papad and pickle
The section an Indian guest scans first, and the one an adapted house menu leaves out. Four to eight of these come with the meal and are not counted against your dish allowance.
Kachumber Salad: chopped cucumber, tomato, onion and lime.
Masala Kachumber Salad: the same, lifted with chaat masala and roasted cumin.
Green Salad: whole cut salad with lemon wedges.
Dhaba Salad: onion rings, green chilli, radish and lime, the roadside version.
Aloo Channa Chat: potato and chickpea, dressed as a chaat.
Kerala Style Chickpeas Salad: chickpeas with coconut and curry leaf.
Mix Raita: yoghurt with cucumber, tomato and onion.
Boondi Raita: gram-flour pearls soaked into spiced yoghurt.
Plain Curd: set yoghurt, served plain for the guests who want it that way.
Masala Papad: crisp papad topped with onion, tomato and chilli.
Roasted Papad: flame-roasted, no oil.
Fresh Mix Pickle Jar: mixed pickle put out by the jar, not in sachets.
Green Chilly Pickle: sharp, for the table that asks for it.
Mango Pickle: the standard oil-cured aam ka achaar.
Coriander Mint Chutney: fresh green chutney ground for the day.
Vegetarian main course: paneer
Paneer, kofta and sabzi are three groups, not one line under the meat. Two to four dishes across the three is the usual count.
Shahi Paneer: paneer in a mild cashew and cream gravy.
Palak Paneer: paneer through a ground spinach base.
Paneer Tikka Butter Masala: tandoori paneer finished in a butter tomato gravy.
Paneer & Capsicum Acharri: pickling spices, peppers and paneer, cooked dry to semi-dry.
Paneer Kundan Qalian: a rich Awadhi-style paneer curry.
Paneer Bhurji: crumbled paneer scrambled with onion and tomato.
Methi Mattar Malai: fenugreek leaves and green peas in a cream gravy.
Vegetarian main course: kofta
The dish that carries a vegetarian buffet when there is room for only one showpiece.
Malai Kofta: paneer and potato dumplings in a cashew gravy.
Veg Kofta Curry: mixed vegetable dumplings in an onion-tomato base.
Kofta Subz Bahar: vegetable koftas in a lighter green gravy.
Vegetarian main course: sabzi
The everyday half of the vegetarian menu, and the half that tells an Indian guest whether a specialist wrote it.
Dum Aloo Bhojpuri: baby potatoes slow-cooked in a sealed pot.
Aloo Gobi: potato and cauliflower, cooked dry.
Aloo Methi Dry: potato with fresh fenugreek.
Aloo Capsicum Dhaba Style: potato and peppers, roadside seasoning.
Tawe Wale Jeera Aloo: cumin potatoes finished on the flat iron.
Gobi Mussalam: whole cauliflower in a rich gravy, a centrepiece dish.
Gobi Gajar Matar: cauliflower, carrot and peas, cooked dry.
Bhendi Do-Pyaza: okra with a double weight of onion.
Aloo Bhindi Masala: okra and potato together.
Baghare Baingan: Hyderabadi aubergine in peanut, sesame and tamarind.
Sarson Ka Saag: Punjabi mustard greens, a winter dish.
Lehsuni Aloo Palak: garlic, potato and spinach.
Hariyali Subz Bahar: mixed vegetables in a green herb gravy.
Subz Miloni: mixed vegetables in a mild North Indian gravy.
Mix Veg Kurma: vegetables in a coconut and cashew kurma.
Veg Kolhapuri: Maharashtrian, and the hottest vegetarian dish on the list.
Kaddu Ka Dalcha: pumpkin cooked with lentils.
Cabbage & Bean Fogath: South Indian dry cabbage with coconut.
Mushroom Masala: mushrooms in an onion-tomato masala.
Sambhar: South Indian lentil and vegetable stew, the partner to the dosa station.
Dal and chole
A menu with one dal on it was written by a generalist. One or two get chosen; this is the range they are chosen from.
Dal Makhani: black lentils cooked overnight with butter and cream.
Dal Tadka: yellow lentils under a ghee and cumin tempering.
Dal Fry: the lighter everyday version, onion and tomato through it.
Dal Amritsari: split black gram, Punjabi seasoning.
Dal Methi: lentils cooked with fresh fenugreek.
Dal Pappu: the plain Andhra lentil, served with rice and ghee.
Dhungar Wali Dal: dal smoked with a live coal at the finish.
Hyderabadi Khatti Dal: sour with tamarind, the Hyderabad standard.
Green Moong Dal: whole green gram, lighter than the rest of this section.
Channa Dal Tadka: split chickpea lentils, tempered.
Lauki Channa Dal: bottle gourd cooked into chana dal.
Panchratan Dal: five lentils in one pot.
Yellow Dal: plain toor dal for a mixed or child-heavy table.
Dhaba Dal: the roadside mixed dal, heavier on garlic.
Dal Khichdi: dal and rice cooked together, also run as a live counter.
Amritsari Chole: dark chickpeas cooked with tea and whole spice.
Pindi Chole: dry-style Rawalpindi chickpeas.
Chana Masala: chickpeas in an onion-tomato masala.
Rajma Masala: red kidney beans, Punjabi style.
Black Channa Curry: kala chana, cooked whole.
Palak Channa: chickpeas through spinach.
Gujrati Kadhi: yoghurt and gram flour, on the sweet side.
Sindhi Kadhi: vegetable and tamarind kadhi, no yoghurt.
Palak Kadhi: spinach folded into a yoghurt kadhi.
Non-vegetarian main course: chicken

Two to four dishes across the three sections below. The regional names carry the weight here: Chettinad, Kolhapuri and Malabar are three different kitchens, and a guest from any of them knows within one bite whether the menu was written by someone who cooks it.
Bombay Butter Chicken: tandoori chicken in a butter and tomato gravy, the safest dish on any menu.
Murgh Lababdar: a richer, slightly sharper cousin of the above.
Malai Chicken Korma: white korma, no chilli heat, built on cashew and cream.
Hyderabadi Murg Korma: korma with whole spice and a deeper colour.
Chicken Chettinad: Tamil, black pepper and roasted coconut, properly hot.
Chicken Ghee Roast: Mangalorean, dry and red with roasted chilli.
Chicken Sukka: coastal Karnataka, dry-cooked with fresh coconut.
Kadai Murg: cooked in the wok with peppers and crushed coriander.
Murg Do Pyaza: chicken carried by onion, twice over.
Murg Khurchan: shredded chicken scraped off the tawa with peppers.
Murg Madras Curry: South Indian, chilli-forward, thin gravy.
Nadan Chicken Curry: Kerala home-style with coconut oil and curry leaf.
Kerala Chicken Ishtu: mild white coconut stew, served with appam or bread.
Kori Gassi: Mangalorean chicken in a roasted coconut gravy.
Dum ka Murg: sealed and slow-cooked in its own steam.
Chicken Methi: chicken with fresh fenugreek.
Chicken Peshawari: dry-style, heavy on tomato and black pepper.
Murgh Musallam: whole stuffed chicken, a centrepiece for a wedding table.
Non-vegetarian main course: lamb and mutton
The section a premium menu is judged on, and the one that needs the longest cook.
Mutton Rogan Josh: Kashmiri, red from chilli and not from tomato.
Rajasthani Lal Maas: mathania chilli, and the hottest dish on this page.
Bhuna Gosht: slow-fried down to a thick coating gravy.
Mutton Kolhapuri: Maharashtrian, dark masala and real heat.
Lamb Xacutti: Goan, roasted coconut and poppy seed.
Sindhi Mutton: onion-heavy, cooked down long.
Keema Mutter: minced mutton with green peas.
Mutton Vindaloo: Goan, vinegar and garlic, sharper than it is hot.
Mutton Korma: mild, cashew and yoghurt based.
Nalli Nihari: overnight shank stew, the dish that needs the most notice.
Sikandari Raan: whole marinated leg of lamb, carved at the table.
Non-vegetarian main course: fish, prawn and egg
One of these on a coastal-leaning menu changes how the whole spread reads.
Goan Fish Curry: tamarind and coconut, sour and hot.
Bengali Fish Curry: mustard-based, cooked light.
Madras Fish Curry: thin, chilli-forward Tamil gravy.
Meen Moilee: Kerala coconut milk stew, mild enough for any table.
Malabar Fish Curry: coconut and kokum, north Kerala.
Pudina Fish Curry: fish in a fresh mint gravy.
Prawn Ghee Roast: Mangalorean, dry and red.
Jhinga Malai Curry: prawns in a mild coconut cream gravy.
Jhinga Masala: prawns in a straight onion-tomato masala.
Egg Do-Pyaza: boiled eggs cooked through a double onion base.
Home-Style Egg Curry: the everyday version, thin gravy.
Egg Ghee Roast: eggs in the Mangalorean roast masala.
Biryani and rice

The dish your guests judge the whole evening on. One on a short menu, two on a premium one, and the Hyderabadi dum biryani earns its place sealed in the handi and opened at the table, not spooned out of a tray.
Kacchi Gosht Ki Biryani: raw marinated mutton and rice sealed and cooked together, the hardest one to get right.
Hyderabadi Mutton Biryani: the benchmark, saffron and fried onion through it.
Handi Hyderabadi Biryani: the same, sealed in the handi and opened at the table.
Dum Murgh Biryani: chicken biryani finished on dum.
Chicken Tikka Biryani with Raita: tandoori chicken layered into the rice.
Dum Tarkari Biryani: the vegetable biryani, sealed and cooked on dum.
Jahangiri Biryani: Mughlai, mild and rich.
Gosht Yakhni Pulao: mutton cooked in its own stock, no chilli.
Murgh Ka Safed Pulao: white chicken pulao for a child-heavy table.
Kashmiri Pulao: sweet, with fruit and nuts.
Zaffrani Pulao: saffron rice, the plainest premium option.
Green Peas Pulao: peas and cumin, the everyday partner to a curry.
Jeera Pulao: cumin rice.
Subz Pulao: mixed vegetable pulao.
Star Anise & Onion Pulao: fried onion and whole spice.
Aloo Gobi Ki Tehri: one-pot rice with potato and cauliflower.
Coconut Rice: South Indian, served alongside the dosa station.
Ghee Bhaat: plain rice finished with ghee.
Steamed Basmati Rice: the one that has to be on the table whatever else is.
Breads from the tandoor
Bread dies in a chafing dish. Two or three types on the menu, and where the venue allows the tandoor they come off it straight onto the plate.
Butter Naan: the default, brushed as it comes off the tandoor.
Garlic Naan: chopped garlic and coriander pressed into the dough.
Chilli Naan: green chilli through it, for the table that wants heat in the bread too.
Methi Naan: fenugreek leaf naan.
Plain Naan: no butter, for a lighter or dairy-light table.
Tandoori Roti: wholewheat, straight onto the tandoor wall.
Missi Roti: gram flour and wheat, Rajasthani.
Makki Ki Roti: maize bread, gluten-free and the partner to sarson ka saag.
Roomali Roti: paper-thin, folded like a handkerchief.
Lachha Paratha: layered and flaky.
Tawa Paratha: plain griddled paratha.
Aloo Paratha: stuffed with spiced potato.
Gobi Paratha: stuffed with cauliflower.
Paneer Paratha: stuffed with crumbled paneer.
Amritsari Kulcha: crisp stuffed kulcha, Punjabi.
Pav: soft rolls for the pav bhaji and vada pav counters.
Bhature: deep-fried and puffed, served with chole.
Puri: small fried bread, the one children eat first.
Mithai and desserts
One dessert on a short menu, two or three on a premium one, and a paan course to close if the room expects it.
Gulab Jamun: served warm, which is the whole point of having a kitchen on site.
Kala Jamun: darker, denser, cooked longer.
Ras Malai: paneer discs in cardamom milk.
Rasgulla: Bengali, light and syrup-soaked.
Jalebi: fried to order at a counter, never trayed.
Malpua: fried pancake soaked in syrup, served with rabdi.
Gajar Halwa: carrot halwa, a winter dessert.
Suji Halwa: semolina halwa, quick and warm.
Moong Dal Halwa: slow-cooked lentil halwa, the richest thing on the list.
Rice Kheer: rice pudding with cardamom.
Vermicelli Kheer: sewai, the Eid version.
Paal Payasam: Kerala milk and rice payasam.
Ada Payasam: rice-flake payasam with jaggery.
Firni: set ground-rice pudding, served chilled in clay.
Rabdi: reduced milk, poured over jalebi or malpua.
Malai Kulfi: dense milk ice, no churn.
Kesar Kulfi: saffron and pistachio kulfi.
Mango Kulfi: mango kulfi, the summer default.
Paan Kulfi: betel leaf kulfi, the closing note.
Kulfi Falooda: kulfi with vermicelli, basil seed and rose.
Kaju Katli: cashew fudge, cut in diamonds (contains nuts)
Milk Cake: grainy set milk fudge.
Peda: soft milk fudge, one bite.
Ghevar: Rajasthani lattice sweet, a festival piece.
Gujiya: stuffed fried pastry, made for Holi.
Chikki: jaggery and peanut brittle (contains nuts)
Saffron Pistachio Baked Yoghurt: the plated-dinner dessert, lighter than mithai (contains nuts)
Modak: steamed or fried, put on the menu for Ganesh Chaturthi.
Live counters
A counter means a chef standing at a station cooking to order, which is a different thing from a tray being topped up. Premium menus carry one or two; weddings run three to five.
Live Tandoor and Roti Station: butter naan, garlic naan, lachha paratha and tandoori roti, hot to the plate.
Live Dum Biryani Station: the sealed handi broken open in front of the guests.
Live Chaat Counter: pani puri, bhel puri, sev puri, papri chaat, dahi puri, dahi bhalla, ragda pattice.
Live Dosa and South Indian Station: plain, masala, ghee roast and cheese dosa with idli, medu vada, sambar and chutneys.
Live Indian Grill: chicken malai tikka, mutton seekh kebab, paneer tikka skewers and grilled prawns with mint chutney.
Tawa Kebab Station: boti and seekh seared on the flat iron.
Live Indo-Chinese Wok: hakka noodles, veg manchurian, chilli chicken, fried rice, spring rolls.
Chole Bhature and Pav Bhaji Counter: the street-food pair, cooked and served at the station.
Sarson da Saag with Makke di Roti Counter: the winter counter, run November to February.
Dal Khichdi Counter: dal khichdi, dal makhani and dal tadka finished at the station.
Live Pani Puri and Sev Puri Station: the chaat counter narrowed to the two dishes that draw a queue.
Jalebi Counter: fried to order and served straight out of the syrup.
Kulfi Falooda Station: kulfi, vermicelli, basil seed and rose, assembled to order.
Gola Station: shaved ice, the one the children stand at.
Paan Counter: sweet and meetha paan made up as guests leave.
The dum biryani reveal is the most photographed moment on an Indian menu in this city, and the dosa station doubles as the strongest Indian breakfast and brunch format.
How many dishes a menu carries

Indian menus in this city are built to a pattern, and knowing it lets you compare two quotes properly. A short menu runs about two starters, three or four mains, two breads, one rice and one dessert. A middle menu adds a welcome drink, a third starter and a second dessert. A premium menu carries four or more starters, five or six mains, three breads, two rice dishes and a live counter. Wedding menus run past a dozen dishes with several counters. Your proposal names the exact count in writing, so you are comparing like with like instead of adjectives.
Vegetarian, Jain, vegan, gluten-free and nut-free
Halal is the baseline across this menu. Beyond that, four things are worth stating plainly instead of promising in general terms.

Pure vegetarian, with separate service lines. A fully vegetarian menu gets built as a menu in its own right — Gujarati, Rajasthani or Sattvic — not as the meat menu with the meat removed. Where a room has both, the vegetarian and non-vegetarian lines are set up and served separately, which most Indian families expect and few caterers commit to in writing.

Jain. Cooked without onion, garlic or root vegetables, on a menu written for it. Dal, kadhi, paneer dishes, rice and most breads carry over; anything built on aloo, gobi or a fried onion base gets replaced, not adapted.

Vegan. Marked dish by dish above, not claimed across the whole menu. Hara bara kebab, pani puri, green pea kachori, vegetable pakora and the vegetable kathi roll are vegan as cooked; the dals, chole, most sabzi and the rice dishes turn vegan when the ghee is swapped for oil, which the chef can do on request.

Gluten-free and nut-free. Rice, biryani, dal, dosa, most curries and makki ki roti suit a gluten-free table; every wheat bread, the samosa and the pakora batter do not. Nut-free is the honest weak spot of this cuisine — korma, malai kofta, kaju katli and most mithai are built on nuts, so a nut-free menu gets designed by leaving those dishes out from the start, not by asking a kitchen to omit them on the night.

Allergen requirements go to the kitchen cooking your event before anything is confirmed. That kitchen assesses its ingredients and its prep environment and tells us what it can and cannot control, and we pass that answer back to you unedited. No menu is described here as free of an allergen unless the chefs responsible for it confirm they can hold that line.
What the venue decides, and what gets checked first

Two parts of this menu depend on the address rather than the budget: the tandoor and live frying. A tandoor works at a villa, outdoors and at ground level on a firm non-combustible base, clear of windows and air-conditioning intakes — and it is confirmed for the specific plot when you book. It never comes inside: Dubai Municipality's barbecue guidance says plainly not to light coal in an enclosed space or indoors, and the UAE Fire Code keeps LPG cylinders out of indoor spaces (11-2.2.6) and off roofs and terraces (Table 11.1). In an apartment or on a yacht it does not run at all. Emaar's vertical-community rules prohibit barbecues, grills or any cooking equipment of any kind on balconies and terraces regardless of fuel, and no LPG cylinder may be brought into a tower or aboard a boat — D-Marin Art. 53.1(a) allows only the vessel's own gas supply, and Dubai Harbour section 7.4 bans operating gas cylinders on marina premises. There the naan, kulcha and tikka bake in the partner's licensed tandoor, travel hot-held, and are finished and brushed in front of guests on an electric or induction station. For a rooftop or a desert site, myCHEF confirms the setup with the building management or the landowner before quoting rather than assuming it.

Live frying works the same way. Jalebi, pakora, samosa and the Amritsari fish are fried on site at a villa, outdoors on a level stable surface and screened from guests, agreed per booking. Indoors in an apartment it is refused, and for a concrete reason: a fryer is a grease-heavy appliance, and Dubai Municipality and Civil Defence expect a Type I extraction hood with wet-chemical suppression above it, which no residential kitchen has. On a boat it fails on the cylinder rule above, plus an open vessel of hot oil on a moving deck. On a beach, lighting a fire outside a designated zone is a Dubai Municipality offence carrying a Dh500 fine, so live frying belongs to a permitted private event or a beach club that has signed it off, not to an open public stretch. The substitute is unglamorous and it works: fry to just short in the licensed kitchen, hold hot, and crisp to order on site — jalebi still comes out of the syrup in front of the guest. Power and water for the live counters get checked the same way. It is a short conversation held with the venue in advance instead of an argument had on the night.
Minimum guest counts

The volume formats — drop-off, working lunch, buffet — start at 10 guests, and 20 guests for a buffet, against a minimum order of AED 900. A chef cooking plated at your table carries no minimum headcount, which is what makes a dinner for six or eight workable where a buffet would not be.

add_block.new_heading: Booking a chef instead of a table
new_paragraphs: Plenty of the people searching for an Indian restaurant in Dubai are not after a table. They want twenty people fed at home in Dubai Hills Estate, a birthday at Dubai Creek Harbour, or a high-end Indian dinner for six without the drive to Downtown and back. A restaurant seats you on its terms: its menu, its two-hour slot, its room, its noise. A chef at your address cooks the same regional food on your timing with the dish list set by you, and the fine dining version of that is a plated tasting at your own table.

Indian catering gets arranged across Dubai Hills Estate and the streets around Dubai Hills Mall, Dubai Creek Harbour, Dubai Festival City, Downtown, Jumeirah, Al Barsha, Mirdif, Palm Jumeirah, Emirates Hills, Business Bay, Dubai Marina and Arabian Ranches. The chef travels with everything the menu needs.

On the two questions people ask before they book: there is no single leading catering company in Dubai for Indian food, and the Indian restaurant in Dubai that wins on a table for two is not the one that wins on feeding sixty people at home. The market splits between hotel banqueting, large wedding caterers and independent chefs, and each wins a different brief. What you can compare is the dish list, the counter list, the minimum guest count, the service format and the itemised price — which is why all five are printed on this page.
Small parties and short guest lists

Indian caterers for small parties are harder to find than caterers for three hundred, because a buffet's economics fight a short guest list. Two routes work. Small party catering in Dubai in the volume formats needs 10 guests, or 20 for a buffet, against the AED 900 minimum order. Under that, a private chef cooking plated has no headcount minimum at all, so a table of six gets a real Indian tasting, not a scaled-down buffet. Ask for the price list both ways and take the cheaper one for your number — at a small party of eight, plated tends to win on cost and on quality at once.

add_block.new_heading: Halal, vegetarian, Jain and spice-level options
new_paragraphs: Dietary needs are designed in, not bolted on. Halal Indian catering is available across the menu — confirm it when you enquire and the chef sources and prepares accordingly. Vegetarian is a strength of Indian cuisine, and we build full plant-forward spreads; see vegetarian catering and, for stricter requirements, Jain catering prepared without onion, garlic or root vegetables. Nut-free, dairy-free and gluten-free adaptations are handled with labelled dishes and separated prep. Spice is set to your crowd, from mild, kid-friendly plates to properly fiery for a table that wants heat. Tell us the mix of guests and we map the menu so vegetarians, meat-eaters and anyone with an allergy all eat well from one table. This is where a matched private Indian chef in Dubai earns their place: the judgement to flex a menu without diluting it.

add_block.new_heading: Planning Indian catering step by step
new_paragraphs: Send your date, guest count and venue — we typically reply within 15 minutes during business hours, with the itemised proposal to follow.

Book as early as you can. A standard buffet or drop-off is often possible at 72 hours , live counters and multi-staff events want 3 to 5 days , and a bespoke wedding menu wants 7 to 14 days . Short-notice requests are assessed individually.
Confirm the menu about 7 days out, with final numbers.
Ask about allergies and Jain or vegan requirements when you enquire, not in the final 48 hours .
Check venue access, power and whether open charcoal is permitted; setup begins about 2 hours before guests arrive.
Plan on roughly 3 hours of service, and add 5% VAT to the total.

new_paragraphs: How much does Indian catering cost in Dubai?

Drop-off and working lunches start at AED 90 per person, a buffet at AED 120, a premium buffet with live counters at AED 150, and a private chef cooking plated at your table runs AED 700 to AED 950 per person. A chef's tasting menu is AED 1400 per person. Minimums are 10 guests for volume formats and 20 for a buffet, with a minimum order of AED 900, and 5% VAT is added to the total.
Do you publish an Indian catering price list?

Yes. Every format has a published starting price per person, with its minimum guest count next to it, so you can price your own event before you send an enquiry. What the list cannot do is guess your menu: the dish count, the number of live counters and the ingredient tier on the proteins move the final figure, and each of those appears as its own line on the proposal.
Which is the best Indian restaurant or Indian caterer in Dubai?

There is no official ranking of either, and a company that awards itself the title is quoting itself. The best Indian restaurant in Dubai for a table for two is rarely the right answer for feeding sixty people at home in Dubai Hills or Downtown, because those are different jobs done by different kinds of kitchen. For catering, judge on what a caterer will tell you before you enquire: the dish list, the number of live counters, the minimum guest count, the service format and a published per-head price. All five are printed on this page, which makes them checkable against anyone else's.
What is the minimum for a small Indian party?

Ten guests for drop-off and working lunches, 20 for a buffet, against a minimum order of AED 900. Below that, a private chef cooking plated has no minimum headcount, so a table of six or eight gets a full Indian menu cooked in front of them at AED 700 to AED 950 per person. For a party of eight, the plated route often costs about the same as forcing a buffet and eats considerably better.
What's included in Indian catering?
Everything: a vetted chef cooking on site, service staff where needed, plating, plus full setup and cleanup. You host; the team runs the kitchen end to end.
Is halal Indian catering available?
Yes — halal options run across the menu. Confirm it when you enquire and the chef sources and prepares accordingly.
Do you cater vegetarian and Jain menus?
Yes. Vegetarian is a strength of Indian cuisine, and full Jain menus are prepared without onion, garlic or root vegetables on request.
Can you adjust the spice level?
Yes. We set heat to your crowd, from mild and kid-friendly to properly fiery, and can vary it dish by dish across one table.
How do I hire Indian catering in Dubai?
Share your date, guest count and venue; we match a vetted chef and send an itemised proposal, usually within one business day.
Do you cater corporate and party events?
Yes — from office Diwali lunches and corporate galas to private parties and weddings. The menu and format are built around the occasion.
For indian catering, the chefs and partner kitchens handling your booking operate to Dubai Municipality food-safety requirements .
Request an Indian catering proposal or chat on WhatsApp . Prefer to browse first? See our sample menus and price guide .
